extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of problem-solving in combinatorics and number theory (undergraduate/olympiad level)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of textbook problems and worked solutions illustrating common proof techniques in combinatorics and elementary number theory (double counting, modular arithmetic, recurrences, parametrizations, existence/nonexistence proofs). Intended as worked examples and methods for contest/undergraduate problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting ("Count Twice")
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities or bounds by counting the same set of objects in two different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: e.g., count committees with a chairman two ways to derive n2^{n-1} (Problem 3.22); count ordered pairs (A,B) or triples (a,b,c) to derive combinatorial identities (Problems 3.28, 3.29); count multiples/divisors to get sums of τ(k), σ(k), φ(k) (Problems 3.31–3.33). The section heading '6.3 Count Twice!' highlights this as a central method. Also exemplified by counting triples in acquaintance graphs (Problem 3.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct additive 'measure' by dyadic weights on a covering
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a function on geometric objects as a convergent weighted sum over a covering so that it is additive on disjoint unions and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.18: cover plane with unit squares U_k and define f(P)=sum_{k>=1} (1/2^k)[P∩U_k]. Because each polygon meets finitely many squares the sum is finite; the 1/2^k weights guarantee f(P)<1 and additivity f(P1∪P2)=f(P1)+f(P2) when interiors disjoint. This is a template for constructing finitely additive bounded set-functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence/nonexistence via geometric packing/area contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a map (or configuration) exists, construct many disjoint small sets whose images must be disjoint, sum their areas and contradict a finite-area bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.17: inscribe a cube in the sphere, partition into n^3 small cubes, take vertices as points whose images must be pairwise separated by ≥1/n, hence disks around images are disjoint; their total area exceeds the containing circle's area for large n, contradiction. General pattern: produce many disjoint objects whose images are disjoint and violate an area/measure constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial bijections / alternative selections
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish equalities by constructing or observing natural bijections between two combinatorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choosing a committee by size vs choosing chairman-first (Problem 3.22); building B by splitting into parts in Problem 3.28. Also used implicitly in counting multiples/divisors for sum identities (Problems 3.31–3.33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic manipulation of generating polynomials (differentiate (1+x)^n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic identities or generating functions and their derivatives to extract combinatorial sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.22: start from (1+x)^n, differentiate and set x=1 to obtain sum k * C(n,k) = n2^{n-1}. Differentiation of binomial expansion is a standard trick to bring down binomial coefficients multiplied by index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform recurrences via auxiliary sequences / Viète relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite nonlinear recurrences into linear ones or derive relations between consecutive terms using algebraic identities (Viète), enabling closed form or integer-preserving properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.40: manipulate given rational recurrence to obtain quadratic whose roots give xn+1 + xn−1 = 10xn, hence linear recurrence xn+1=10xn−xn−1 and integrality by induction. Viète relations are used to deduce linear recurrences from quadratic relations between terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize known sequences and prove by induction / closed form
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify that a sequence matches a known sequence (e.g., Fibonacci), posit closed form (e.g., x_n=F_n^2) and verify by induction or via characteristic roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.38: observe initial terms correspond to squares of Fibonacci numbers and prove xn=F_n^2 by induction. Problem 3.44: use closed-form roots α,β to express xn and deduce squares after algebraic manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametrize solutions by factoring and gcd decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor equations and set x= d a, y = d b with gcd(a,b)=1 to deduce divisibility relations and parametrize all integer solutions in terms of free parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.48: rewrite x(x−z)=y(y−x), set d=gcd(x,y), x=da,y=db and deduce linear relations producing x=ma^2, y=mab, z=m(a^2+ab−b^2) for arbitrary m,a,b. This is standard: factor, extract gcd, use coprimality to push divisibility to parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity and modular arithmetic to rule out integer solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze congruences and quadratic residues modulo small moduli to show impossibility or force divisibility that yields contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: Problem 3.62 uses quadratic residues and Fermat to deduce prime divisors ≡1 mod 4 contradiction; Problem 3.68 checks RHS ≡7 (mod 8) and notes sum of three squares can't be ≡7 (mod 8); Problem 3.64 uses residues modulo 7 to force all variables divisible by 7 contradiction. General method: compute residues, use known classification of square residues, or Fermat/Euler criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding via combinatorial/geometric counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain lower and upper bounds for counts of combinatorial/geometric objects and compare to deduce inequalities or contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.30: lower bound on number of isosceles triangles from each vertex (n*k/2) and upper bound per pair ≤2 leads to inequality k(k−1) ≤ 2(n−1) and final bound k < √(2n)+1/2. Typical pattern: count the same family with two different estimates (one local, one global).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct infinite families via algebraic identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use polynomial identities or simple algebraic equalities to produce parametrized infinite families of integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.53: (a+1)^4−(a−1)^4 = 8a^3+8a and choose a=b^3 with b even to produce infinite primitive quadruples; Problem 3.58 uses (n+1)^3+(n−1)^3−2n^3=6n to give infinite solutions. The template: find identity expressing desired RHS in terms of simple expressions and parametrize integer choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce degree by fixing a factor (set x−z=1 or similar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix one factor to a convenient small integer to reduce a Diophantine equation to a simpler linear or quadratic form which can be solved and then parametrized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.49: choose x−z=1 to obtain 2x−1 + y^2 = n and then set y suitably to make x integer; general trick: choose a small divisor or factor to simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis on parity/odd-even structure of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Split into cases depending on parities of variables (all even/all odd/mixed) and treat separately, often reducing by dividing by 2 when all even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.52: analyze whether a,b,c,d are odd or even; if all even, divide by 2^2 and iterate recursively; if odd, deduce n=1. This recursive parity descent is common in sum-of-powers Diophantine problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform problem to checking small possibilities via strong inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive inequalities that force variables into small finite sets, then check those possibilities exhaustively to reach contradiction or list solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.67: derive (x_k−1)^4 ≤ 14 forcing each x_k∈{1,2}, then plug values to get contradiction. Use when global inequality tightly bounds each variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative generation of larger solutions from a base solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Given one integral solution, use algebraic transformation (often Vieta- or composition-based) to produce a strictly larger solution, iterating to get infinitely many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.56: from one solution of ax^2−by^2=1 produce a larger solution by an explicit algebraic formula; Problem 3.57: from (x,y) generate (4y−1−x,y), increasing sum, thus infinite chain starting from (1,1). This is the 'bootstrap' approach to infinite families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting via binary matrix row/column sums (double-count in arrays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent integer sequences or inequalities as counts of 1's in a 0–1 matrix and count by rows vs columns to relate two summations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.26: define n×m binary array with first a_i entries 1 in row i; counting 1's by rows gives sum a_i, by columns gives sum b_j, yielding equality. This is a standard bijective/double-count array technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of substitution a = x−y, b = x+y to symmetrize
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply linear substitutions to exploit symmetry and reduce to simpler Diophantine forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.55: set a = x−y, b = x+y to rewrite x^2+y^2=(x−y)^3 as a^2+b^2=2a^3 and then parametrize. This substitution often linearizes or isolates factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit limited number of solutions modulo small primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute possible residues of terms (e.g., squares, cubes, higher powers) modulo a small prime and show RHS cannot be matched, proving no integer solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.69 (partial): reduce to checking both sides modulo 19, note z^9 ≡ ±1 if z not divisible by 19, and compare with possible square residues to exclude values 13 and 14 modulo 19. Use lists of quadratic residues and Fermat to eliminate possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiplicative structure and coprimality constraints to force parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coprimality facts (gcd bounds) to force factors to be powers or particular forms, reducing to studying m small or specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 3.50 and 3.51: deduce 1+4y^{m−1} must be an odd square, factor ym−1 = a(a+1) then coprimality of a and a+1 forces each to be (m−1)th powers, giving constraints that force m to specific values and thereby solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole / index-doubling to create long zero-runs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_n ≥ a_{2n}+a_{2n+1} and some term is zero then repeatedly doubling index yields arbitrarily long consecutive zero blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.45: show at least one term is zero (else a1≥2^n → contradiction), then from ak=0 deduce a_{2^n k}=...=a_{2^n k + 2^n −1}=0 giving 2^n consecutive zeros; hence for any N choose n with 2^n≥N. Pattern: use binary expansion/doubling indices to expand zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive identities by manipulating sums over permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum a quantity over all permutations and evaluate the sum in two ways (by symmetry and by modular counting) to obtain congruences or contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.25: consider S(a)=sum c_i a_i over permutations a; assume all S(a) distinct mod n! leads to contradiction by comparing computed total in two ways and using divisibility properties since n is odd. Useful when symmetric sums over permutations can be explicitly counted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recursion/induction on easily computable differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Define difference sequence b_n=a_{n+1}−a_n to obtain simpler arithmetic progression or recurrence, sum back to obtain closed form for a_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.42: from an+1−an=b_n with b_n linear, get b_n=b_0+2n, sum to get an = n^2−n+1 and verify multiplicative identity. Good when successive differences are simpler than original sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small-factor multiplicative constraints to force contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that prime divisors must satisfy incompatible congruence conditions (e.g., all primes dividing something are ≡1 (mod 4) yet parity contradicts), yielding impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.62: prime p dividing 4x−1 must satisfy (2z)^2 ≡−1 (mod p) so p≡1 (mod 4), hence 4x−1≡1 (mod 4) contradiction. Pattern: derive congruence condition on prime divisors, then reach modular impossibility.
